questiontext.text: What is the greatest common divisor of 24 and 36?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. The divisors of 24 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24. Of these, 12 also divides 36, and nothing larger does.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
int a = 84, b = 36;
while (b != 0) {
    int r = a % b;
    a = b;
    b = r;
}
cout << a << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. The pairs are (84, 36), then (36, 12), then (12, 0). When b becomes 0 the answer is a = 12.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text: Which relation is the heart of Euclid's algorithm?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. The common divisors of a and b are exactly the common divisors of b and a % b, so the pair can be replaced by a smaller one.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
cout << gcd(0, 5) << " " << gcd(17, 0) << " " << gcd(12, 12) << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Every number divides zero, so gcd(0, x) = x and gcd(x, 0) = x. And gcd(12, 12) = 12.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text: About how many steps does Euclid's algorithm need for two numbers near a billion?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. The number of steps grows like log n, so even the worst case needs only a few dozen steps.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. The condition is tested first, then the remainder is computed from the old values. Only after that do a and b change, and the answer is printed at the end.

questiontext.text: How do we compute the least common multiple of a and b safely?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. We divide first and multiply second. This keeps the intermediate number small and avoids overflow.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
long long a = 12, b = 18;
cout << gcd(a, b) * lcm(a, b) << " " << a * b << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. gcd(12, 18) = 6 and lcm(12, 18) = 36, and their product 216 equals 12 * 18.

questiontext.text: What is the least common multiple of 4, 6 and 10?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. lcm(4, 6) = 12, then lcm(12, 10) = 60. The number 60 is divisible by all three.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text:
Match each problem with the tool that solves it.

Drag each description onto the item it belongs to.

The largest square tile that covers a rectangle without cutting  →  [[1]]

When two blinking lights flash together again  →  [[2]]

Reducing the fraction 18/24  →  [[3]]

Adding 1/6 and 3/10  →  [[4]]

Two numbers whose gcd is 1  →  [[5]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. The gcd looks for the largest shared divisor, and the lcm for the first shared multiple. Each of these situations is one of the two.

The correct answer:

  • The largest square tile that covers a rectangle without cutting → gcd
  • When two blinking lights flash together again → lcm
  • Reducing the fraction 18/24 → Dividing by the gcd
  • Adding 1/6 and 3/10 → Using the lcm as the denominator
  • Two numbers whose gcd is 1 → Coprime numbers

questiontext.text: A floor of 360 by 240 is covered with the largest possible square tiles with no cutting. How many tiles are needed?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. The side is gcd(360, 240) = 120. That gives 3 tiles along the length and 2 along the width, so 6 tiles.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

name.text: Q14 - Drag and drop - fill the gaps

questiontext.text:
Drag the correct condition into the gap so the loop stops at the right moment and the program prints 4.

main.cpp
int a = 20, b = 8;
while (b [[1]] 0) {
    int r = a % b;
    a = b;
    b = r;
}
cout << a << endl;

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. We keep looping while b is not zero. The pairs are (20, 8), (8, 4), (4, 0), so the answer is 4. With == the loop would never start and the program would print 20.

The correct answer:

main.cpp
int a = 20, b = 8;
while (b != 0) {
    int r = a % b;
    a = b;
    b = r;
}
cout << a << endl;

questiontext.text:
Match each expression with its meaning.

Drag each description onto the item it belongs to.

a % b  →  [[1]]

gcd(a, 0)  →  [[2]]

a / gcd(a, b) * b  →  [[3]]

gcd(a, b) == 1  →  [[4]]

swap(a, b)  →  [[5]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. These are the small pieces that every gcd and lcm program is made of.

The correct answer:

  • a % b → The remainder of a divided by b
  • gcd(a, 0) → a
  • a / gcd(a, b) * b → The least common multiple
  • gcd(a, b) == 1 → a and b are coprime
  • swap(a, b) → Exchanges the two values

Arrange the lines so the program prints 21.

Drag the lines into the order the computer runs them.

order the lines

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. The loop needs both values first. Inside it, a %= b takes the remainder and swap exchanges the roles, and the answer is printed after the loop.

The correct answer:

main.cpp
int a = 252, b = 105;
while (b != 0) {
    a %= b;
    swap(a, b);
}
cout << a << endl;

questiontext.text: Two alarms ring every 12 and every 15 minutes and have just rung together. When do they next ring together?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. We need the least common multiple: 12 / 3 * 15 = 60.
